why: Airflow is the most common orchestrator in data engineering job offers. It schedules pipelines, retries failures and shows what ran when.
outcome: write a DAG with dependent tasks, schedule it, pass data between tasks correctly and debug a failed run.

lessons.title: DAGs, tasks and schedules
text: A DAG (directed acyclic graph) is a pipeline: tasks and the order they run in. Airflow reads Python files in the dags folder and runs each DAG on its schedule.
Each run has a logical date (the data interval it processes). Pipelines should process that interval, not 'now', so re-running an old day gives the same result.
points: schedule='@daily' or a cron string like '0 6 * * *' (every day at 06:00).
catchup=False avoids running every missed interval since start_date.
retries and retry_delay handle temporary failures.
Tasks should be idempotent: running them twice gives the same result.

example.note: TaskFlow API (Airflow 2+). ds is the run's logical date as YYYY-MM-DD.

lessons.title: Operators, connections and passing data
text: Operators are ready-made task types: BashOperator, PythonOperator, SQL operators, cloud transfers. Connections store credentials (database, cloud) outside the code.
Tasks pass small values through XCom (what @task functions return). Large data never goes through XCom: write it to storage and pass the path.
points: Set dependencies with >>: extract >> transform >> load.
Create connections in the UI (Admin → Connections) or with environment variables.
Variables hold small configuration; never put secrets in DAG code.
Use templating ({{ ds }}) to inject the run date into SQL or commands.

example.code:
from airflow.operators.bash import BashOperator
from airflow.providers.common.sql.operators.sql import SQLExecuteQueryOperator

download = BashOperator(
    task_id="download",
    bash_command="python /opt/jobs/download.py --date {{ ds }}",
)
aggregate = SQLExecuteQueryOperator(
    task_id="aggregate",
    conn_id="warehouse",
    sql="INSERT INTO daily_offers SELECT '{{ ds }}', COUNT(*) FROM raw_offers WHERE day = '{{ ds }}'",
)
download >> aggregate

lessons.title: Run, monitor and debug
text: The UI shows each DAG run and the state of every task. When something fails, open the task logs first: most errors are a missing connection, a wrong path or bad input data.
After fixing, clear the failed task (and downstream tasks) to re-run only what is needed.
points: airflow dags test <dag_id> 2026-10-01 runs a DAG once locally without the scheduler.
airflow tasks test <dag_id> <task_id> <date> runs a single task.
Backfill re-runs past intervals after a bug fix.
Alert on failure (email, Slack callback) so you are not the last to know.

example.code:
airflow dags list
airflow dags test job_offers 2026-10-01
airflow tasks test job_offers load 2026-10-01

lessons.title: Production DAGs: idempotency, backfills and retries
text: A task will run more than once: retries after a timeout, a manual re-run, a backfill of past dates. Make every task idempotent: running it twice for the same date gives the same result. Replace the partition for the run's logical date instead of appending, and use the date Airflow gives you, not datetime.now().

A backfill runs the DAG for past dates, for example after fixing a bug. With idempotent tasks it is safe. Add retries with a delay for flaky sources, timeouts so a stuck task does not block the day, and alerts on failure so someone knows.
points: Use the logical date ({{ ds }} or the ds argument) to select the data of the run.
catchup=False avoids an accidental flood of runs when a DAG is first deployed.
retries + retry_delay handle temporary errors; execution_timeout stops stuck tasks.
Keep heavy processing out of the scheduler: push it to the warehouse, Spark or a container.

example.note: Delete then insert for the run date: running the task twice gives the same table.

lessons.title: Logical date, data intervals and catchup
text: Every scheduled DAG run covers a data interval. With the classic Airflow 2 behaviour, the daily run with logical date 2026-10-01 covers 2026-10-01 00:00 to 2026-10-02 00:00 and starts just after that interval ends, on 2 October. This surprises everyone once: the run 'for' a day happens the day after, because only then is that day's data complete.

Inside tasks, use data_interval_start and data_interval_end (or ds, the logical date as YYYY-MM-DD) to select the rows of the run. Filtering on a half-open range, >= start and < end, never misses or double counts a row at midnight, and it keeps working if you later switch to hourly runs.

catchup decides what happens to the intervals between start_date and today that never ran. With catchup=True the scheduler creates one run per missing interval as soon as the DAG is switched on: useful for a planned history load, painful by accident. Airflow 3 defaults catchup to False, Airflow 2 to True (unless catchup_by_default was changed), so set it explicitly in every DAG.

Airflow 3 changes a few details. A plain cron schedule now uses CronTriggerTimetable by default: the run starts at the cron time and its data interval is a single point, so set [scheduler] create_cron_data_intervals = True or use CronDataIntervalTimetable when your tasks rely on intervals. Manual and asset-triggered runs can have no logical date, old context names such as execution_date, next_ds and prev_ds are removed, and backfills are created with airflow backfill create and run by the scheduler instead of the CLI process.
points: data_interval_start / data_interval_end: the exact window a scheduled run should process.
Filter with >= start AND < end: no gap and no overlap between runs.
Set catchup explicitly: True for a planned history load, False otherwise.
Backfill in Airflow 2: airflow dags backfill -s D1 -e D2 <dag>; in Airflow 3: airflow backfill create --dag-id <dag> --from-date D1 --to-date D2.
Use a fixed, timezone-aware start_date (pendulum) so intervals are predictable.

example.code:
import pendulum
from airflow.decorators import dag, task
from airflow.timetables.interval import CronDataIntervalTimetable

# explicit data intervals: same behaviour in Airflow 2 and 3
@dag(schedule=CronDataIntervalTimetable("0 0 * * *", timezone="Europe/Paris"),
     start_date=pendulum.datetime(2026, 1, 1, tz="Europe/Paris"),
     catchup=False, max_active_runs=1)
def offers_by_interval():
    @task
    def load(data_interval_start=None, data_interval_end=None):
        window = f"loaded_at >= '{data_interval_start}' AND loaded_at < '{data_interval_end}'"
        run_sql(f"DELETE FROM offers_daily WHERE {window}")
        run_sql(f"INSERT INTO offers_daily SELECT * FROM raw_offers WHERE {window}")
    load()

offers_by_interval()
example.note: The same half-open window in the delete and the insert: re-runs are idempotent and runs never overlap. In Airflow 3, dag and task can also be imported from airflow.sdk.

lessons.title: TaskFlow, XCom limits and dynamic task mapping
text: With the TaskFlow API, the return value of a @task function is pushed to XCom, and passing it to another task both creates the dependency and pulls the value. It reads like plain Python, but each task still runs separately, maybe on another machine: the value travels through Airflow's metadata database (or a configured XCom backend), serialised.

That is why XCom is for small things: a file path, a row count, a list of dates, a few ids. Pushing a DataFrame or a large list makes the metadata database grow, slows the UI and can fail on size or serialisation. Write the data to object storage or a table, return its location, and let the next task read it. If you really must move bigger objects, a custom XCom backend that stores values in object storage keeps only a reference in the database.

Dynamic task mapping (Airflow 2.3+) creates one task instance per element of a list that is only known at run time: one per file that arrived, per country, per customer. Call .expand() on the task with the list, and .partial() for the arguments that are the same for every copy. Each mapped instance has its own logs, retries and state, so you can clear only the one that failed.

Keep mapped lists bounded. Airflow caps a mapped task at max_map_length instances (1024 by default), and hundreds of tiny tasks cost more in scheduling than they save. Group work into batches when the list can be long, and set max_active_tis_per_dag on the task to protect a fragile API from too many parallel calls.
points: @task(multiple_outputs=True) returning a dict pushes each key as its own XCom.
Return a path or an id, never the data itself.
task.partial(fixed=...).expand(varying=list) creates one instance per element.
The task after a mapped task receives the list of all mapped results.
In Airflow 3, import dag and task from airflow.sdk; task code can no longer query the metadata database directly.

example.note: Three load instances run (two at a time), each with its own logs and retries.

lessons.title: Sensors, deferrable operators and data-aware scheduling
text: A sensor is a task that waits for a condition: a file in a bucket, a row in a table, a task in another DAG. In the default mode='poke' it holds a worker slot the whole time it waits, so ten sensors waiting all night can block real work. mode='reschedule' releases the slot between checks and suits long waits with a large poke_interval.

Deferrable operators go further. With deferrable=True, on the operators and sensors that support it, the task hands its wait to the triggerer, a separate Airflow process that watches many conditions at once with asyncio, and frees the worker completely until the event fires. A triggerer must be running (airflow triggerer); managed services and the official Docker Compose setup usually start one.

Always give sensors a timeout: the default is seven days, so a file that never arrives keeps a task waiting for a week. Decide what a missing input means: fail and alert, or soft_fail=True to mark the sensor skipped so the run ends quietly.

Often you do not need to wait at all. Data-aware scheduling triggers a DAG when another DAG has updated some data: the producer task declares outlets, and the consumer DAG uses that dataset as its schedule. It is called Dataset in Airflow 2.4+ and Asset in Airflow 3 (from airflow.sdk import Asset). It replaces many cross-DAG sensors and shows the dependency in the UI.
points: poke_interval: seconds between checks; timeout: total seconds before giving up.
mode='reschedule' frees the worker between checks; deferrable=True frees it completely.
Deferrable tasks need the triggerer process to be running.
soft_fail=True marks the sensor skipped instead of failed when it times out.
Dataset (Airflow 2) / Asset (Airflow 3): schedule a DAG on data updates, not on a clock.

example.note: offers_reporting has no clock: it runs each time load succeeds and updates the dataset.

lessons.title: Connections, secrets and testing DAGs before production
text: Credentials never belong in a DAG file. A connection stores host, login, password and extras under a conn_id, and tasks and hooks only know that id. Connections can live in the metadata database (UI or CLI), in environment variables named AIRFLOW_CONN_<ID>, or in a secrets backend such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager or GCP Secret Manager, which Airflow checks first. Variables (AIRFLOW_VAR_<NAME> or the UI) hold small settings such as a bucket name or a list of countries.

Read variables inside tasks or templates ({{ var.value.bucket }}), not at the top of the file: top-level code runs at every parse, and each Variable.get there is a database or secrets-backend call. Airflow masks in logs the passwords of connections and the values of variables whose name contains words like password, secret or api_key, but printing a secret stored under another name will leak it.

Test DAGs like code. A DAG integrity test loads every file with DagBag and fails on import errors or cycles, plus any rule you add (tags, retries, owner); it catches most broken deployments in CI in seconds. dag.test() and airflow dags test run a whole DAG in one process for a given date, which is ideal for debugging with breakpoints. Keep business logic in plain Python functions so you can unit-test it without Airflow at all.

Production failures repeat: a slow DAG file that times out while being parsed, a naive start_date that runs at an unexpected hour, tasks stuck in queued because a pool or max_active_tasks is full, a worker killed for lack of memory that leaves a task failed with almost no log, an expired credential. Read the task log, then the scheduler and worker logs, before changing code.
points: AIRFLOW_CONN_WAREHOUSE='postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/db' defines a connection from the environment.
Look-up order: secrets backend, then environment variables, then the metadata database.
Read variables in templates or task code, never with a top-level Variable.get.
DagBag(include_examples=False).import_errors == {} is the first test to run in CI.
airflow dags list-import-errors shows the files that failed to parse.

example.note: Run it in an environment with the same Airflow version and providers as production.

items: c waits for a and b
Cron schedule with real data intervals
Limit parallel copies of a task
Give up after 1 h and skip
Run when data is updated (Asset in Airflow 3)

pitfalls: Heavy code at the top level of the DAG file (API calls, queries): it runs every time the scheduler parses the file.
Using datetime.now() inside tasks instead of the logical date, which breaks re-runs.
Dynamic start_date (datetime.now()) that makes the DAG never run.
Reading Variables or connections at the top level of a DAG file: one database or secrets call at every parse.
Sensors in poke mode with the default seven-day timeout, quietly holding worker slots.
Assuming a cron schedule gives the same data interval after upgrading to Airflow 3: check the timetable.

exercises.q: Write the dependency line for: extract runs first, then clean and enrich in parallel, then load.
A daily DAG failed for 3 days because of a bug, now fixed. How do you re-process those days?
exercises.answer: Clear the failed runs in the UI (with downstream tasks) or run a backfill for that date range: airflow dags backfill -s 2026-10-01 -e 2026-10-03 <dag_id>. This works because tasks use the logical date and are idempotent.

exercises.q: Write a cron schedule for every Monday at 07:30.
A bug corrupted the sales of 1 to 7 March. The code is fixed. Re-run those days with the CLI.
exercises.hint: airflow dags backfill with start and end dates.

exercises.q: A daily DAG with classic Airflow 2 intervals has a run with logical date 2026-10-14. When does it start, and which time window should it load?
exercises.answer: It starts just after 2026-10-15 00:00, when its interval ends. It should load from data_interval_start (2026-10-14 00:00) included to data_interval_end (2026-10-15 00:00) excluded: filter with >= start and < end.

exercises.q: Use dynamic task mapping to run process(path, table) once per path returned by list_paths(), with the same table 'staging' for every copy.
exercises.hint: partial() for the fixed argument, expand() for the list.

exercises.q: A sensor waits up to 12 hours every night for a partner file and blocks a worker slot. Rewrite it so it does not occupy a worker and skips the run if the file never arrives.
exercises.answer:
S3KeySensor(
    task_id="wait_partner_file",
    bucket_name="partner",
    bucket_key="exports/{{ ds }}/data.csv",
    deferrable=True,
    poke_interval=600,
    timeout=12 * 60 * 60,
    soft_fail=True,
)

exercises.q: With Airflow 3, write the command that re-runs only the failed runs of sales_daily between 1 and 7 March 2026.
exercises.hint: airflow backfill create with a reprocess behaviour.

interview.q: What does idempotent mean for a pipeline task?
interview.a: Running it several times for the same interval gives the same result, for example by overwriting the partition for that date instead of appending. It makes retries and backfills safe.

interview.q: What is XCom and when should you avoid it?
interview.a: A mechanism to pass small values between tasks, stored in Airflow's metadata database. Avoid it for large data such as DataFrames or files: write them to storage and pass the path.
Cron only triggers commands at times. Airflow adds dependencies between tasks, retries, backfills, a UI with history and logs, and connections management.

interview.q: What does idempotent mean for a data pipeline task, and how do you achieve it?
interview.a: Running the task several times for the same input period gives the same result, with no duplicates. I achieve it by processing a well-defined partition (the run's logical date), overwriting or merging that partition instead of appending, using upserts with keys, and avoiding side effects based on the current time.

interview.q: What are data_interval_start and data_interval_end, and why does a daily run start the day after its date?
interview.a: They bound the period of data a scheduled run must process. With interval-based schedules, the run for 14 October covers 14 October 00:00 to 15 October 00:00 and starts once that period is over, because only then is the data complete. In Airflow 3, plain cron schedules run at the cron time by default, so I check the timetable and use explicit intervals when tasks depend on them.

interview.q: Sensor in poke mode, reschedule mode or deferrable: what is the difference?
interview.a: Poke keeps a worker slot for the whole wait. Reschedule frees the slot between checks and re-schedules the sensor, good for long waits. Deferrable hands the wait to the triggerer process, which watches many conditions asynchronously, so no worker is used until the event happens. In every case I set a timeout and decide between failing and soft_fail.

interview.q: How would you pass a 2 GB result from one task to the next?
interview.a: Not through XCom, which lives in the metadata database and is meant for small values. The first task writes the result to object storage or a warehouse table, partitioned by the run's date, and returns the path or table name; the next task reads from there. For many inputs I would use dynamic task mapping over the list of paths.

interview.q: How do you test Airflow DAGs before they reach production?
interview.a: A DAG integrity test in CI that loads every file with DagBag and fails on import errors, plus team rules such as retries and tags. Unit tests on the business logic kept in plain Python functions. Then airflow dags test or dag.test() for a real date in a development environment with the same Airflow version, connections pointing to test resources.
